claim: LINE-1 (L1) is the only autonomously active retrotransposon in the human genome.
source: LINE-1 (L1) is the only autonomously active retrotransposon in the human genome, and accounts for 17% of the human genome.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and introduction as an established fact about L1.

claim: LINE-1 accounts for 17% of the human genome.
source: LINE-1 (L1) is the only autonomously active retrotransposon in the human genome, and accounts for 17% of the human genome.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is a well-established genomic fact.

claim: The L1 mRNA encodes two proteins, ORF1p and ORF2p, both essential for retrotransposition.
source: The L1 mRNA encodes two proteins, ORF1p and ORF2p, both essential for retrotransposition.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: ORF2p has reverse transcriptase and endonuclease activities.
source: ORF2p has reverse transcriptase and endonuclease activities, while ORF1p is a homotrimeric RNA-binding protein with poorly understood function.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Feng et al., 1996; Cost et al., 2002; Mathias et al., 1991).

claim: ORF1p is a homotrimeric RNA-binding protein.
source: ORF2p has reverse transcriptase and endonuclease activities, while ORF1p is a homotrimeric RNA-binding protein with poorly understood function.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Martin and Bushman, 2001; Martin et al., 2005).

claim: Condensation of ORF1p is critical for L1 retrotransposition.
source: Here, we show that condensation of ORF1p is critical for L1 retrotransposition.
evidence: This is the main claim of the paper, supported by experimental data showing that mutations preventing condensation abolish retrotransposition.

claim: Electrostatic interactions and trimer conformational dynamics together tune the properties of ORF1p assemblies to allow for efficient L1 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complex formation in cells.
source: Using a combination of biochemical reconstitution and live-cell imaging, we demonstrate that electrostatic interactions and trimer conformational dynamics together tune the properties of ORF1p assemblies to allow for efficient L1 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complex formation in cells.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro and cellular experiments showing salt-dependent condensation and the role of the coiled-coil stammer motif.

claim: Mutations that prevented ORF1p condensation led to loss of retrotransposition activity.
source: Mutations that prevented ORF1p condensation led to loss of retrotransposition activity, while orthogonal restoration of coiled-coil conformational flexibility rescued both condensation and retrotransposition.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the K3A/K4A, R261A, and StammerDel mutants which show loss of both condensation and retrotransposition.

claim: Orthogonal restoration of coiled-coil conformational flexibility rescued both condensation and retrotransposition.
source: Mutations that prevented ORF1p condensation led to loss of retrotransposition activity, while orthogonal restoration of coiled-coil conformational flexibility rescued both condensation and retrotransposition.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the StammerAAA and StammerAEA mutants which restore condensation and retrotransposition activity.

claim: Dynamic ORF1p oligomerization on L1 RNA drives the formation of an L1 RNP condensate that is essential for retrotransposition.
source: Based on these observations, we propose that dynamic ORF1p oligomerization on L1 RNA drives the formation of an L1 RNP condensate that is essential for retrotransposition.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental observations in the paper.

claim: L1 drives propagation of non-autonomous retrotransposons and processed pseudogenes, which make up an additional 21% of the human genome.
source: L1 also drives propagation of non-autonomous retrotransposons and processed pseudogenes, which make up an additional 21% of the human genome (Lander et al., 2001; Jurka, 1997; Dewannieux et al., 2003; Kazazian and Moran, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Full-length, retrotransposition-competent L1s are 6 kilobases (kb) in length.
source: While the majority of genomic human L1s have undergone truncations and mutations that have rendered them inactive, full-length, retrotransposition-competent L1s are 6 kilobases (kb) in length and have a 5' untranslated region (UTR) containing a bidirectional promoter, two open reading frames (ORFs), ORF1 and ORF2, separated by a short inter-ORF linker, and a 3' UTR with a weak polyadenylation signal (Figure 1A; Speek, 2001; Swergold, 1990; Dombroski et al., 1991; Doucet et al., 2015; Burns and Boeke, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: ORF1p contains three structured domains: a coiled coil (CC) that mediates trimerization, an RNA recognition motif (RRM), and a C-terminal domain (CTD) that cooperates with the RRM to bind nucleic acids.
source: ORF1p contains three structured domains, a coiled coil (CC) that mediates trimerization, an RNA recognition motif (RRM), and a C-terminal domain (CTD) that cooperates with the RRM to bind nucleic acids (Figure 1A–B; Januszyk et al., 2007; Khazina and Weichenrieder, 2009; Khazina et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and shown in Figure 1A-B, supported by citations.

claim: The N-terminal region (NTR) is the first 52 residues of ORF1p and is unstructured.
source: The N-terminal region (NTR) is the first 52 residues of ORF1p. This region is unstructured and contains phosphorylation sites and a basic charged patch that are necessary for retrotransposition (Adney et al., 2019; Cook et al., 2015; Khazina and Weichenrieder, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The NTR contains phosphorylation sites and a basic charged patch that are necessary for retrotransposition.
source: The N-terminal region (NTR) is the first 52 residues of ORF1p. This region is unstructured and contains phosphorylation sites and a basic charged patch that are necessary for retrotransposition (Adney et al., 2019; Cook et al., 2015; Khazina and Weichenrieder, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: ORF1p expressed from a full-length active L1 element rapidly forms cytoplasmic condensates in cells.
source: Here, we demonstrate that ORF1p expressed from a full-length active L1 element rapidly forms cytoplasmic condensates in cells that exhibit cis preference.
evidence: This is demonstrated by live-cell imaging experiments showing puncta formation after 6 hours of induction.

claim: ORF1p condensates exhibit cis preference.
source: Here, we demonstrate that ORF1p expressed from a full-length active L1 element rapidly forms cytoplasmic condensates in cells that exhibit cis preference.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-expression experiments showing minimal mixing of differently tagged ORF1p proteins.

claim: After 6 hr of L1 induction, ORF1-Halo forms bright, punctate, and highly uniform structures against a weaker background of diffuse ORF1-Halo signal.
source: After 6 hr of L1 induction using the Tet-On system in HeLa cells, we noted the formation of bright, punctate, and highly uniform ORF1-Halo structures against a weaker background of diffuse ORF1-Halo signal (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ORF1p puncta appear as early as three hours following induction with doxycycline.
source: These foci were absent without induction, appeared as early as three hours following induction with doxycycline, and increased in number, but not size, with induction times up to 24 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is shown in the time course experiments in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: ORF1p puncta increase in number, but not size, with induction times up to 24 hr.
source: These foci were absent without induction, appeared as early as three hours following induction with doxycycline, and increased in number, but not size, with induction times up to 24 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is shown in the time course experiments in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Nuclear ORF1-Halo puncta have approximately 25 times lower diffusivity compared to cytoplasmic puncta.
source: Nuclear ORF1-Halo puncta had similar morphology and fluorescence intensity but very different diffusion behavior compared to cytoplasmic puncta (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E): diffusivity was approximately 25 times higher for cytoplasmic puncta (Video 1).
evidence: This is quantified from particle tracking experiments shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: ORF1p from co-expressed L1s predominantly condense separately in singly-labeled foci.
source: We almost always found singly-labeled puncta and only rarely observed puncta that contained both ORF1-Halo and ORF1-mNG2 (Video 2).
evidence: This is shown in the colocalization experiments in Figure 1E-F and Video 2.

claim: 21% of JF549+ spots had detectable mNG2, compared to 56% with detectable JF646 signal.
source: However, there was occasional mNG2 signal at JF549+ spots: 21% of JF549+ had detectable mNG2, compared to 56% with detectable JF646 signal (detection defined as an intensity three standard deviations above the median intensity of random spots, Materials and methods).
evidence: This is quantified from the colocalization analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: 41% of ORF1 puncta are positive for RNA signal compared to 10% of random spots.
source: By staining for ORF1-Halo and performing hybridized chain reaction RNA fluorescence in situ hybridization (HCR-RNA FISH; Choi et al., 2018) for the HaloTag sequence specific to our exogenously introduced L1 in the same cells, we found that cytoplasmic ORF1 puncta were often enriched for cis L1 RNA signal, with 41% of ORF1 puncta being positive for RNA signal compared to 10% of random spots (Figure 1G, Materials and methods).
evidence: This is quantified from the RNA FISH experiments shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Purified ORF1p forms an extensive condensed phase at low micromolar protein concentrations in buffer with physiological pH and salt concentrations.
source: Purified ORF1p protein formed an extensive condensed phase at low micromolar protein concentrations in buffer with physiological pH and salt concentrations (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in the in vitro condensation assays in Figure 2A.

claim: No ORF1p condensate formation is observed above 300 mM KCl.
source: When the same concentration of protein was incubated in buffers with increasing salt concentrations, the mean intensity of the protein in the condensed phase, the partition coefficient of the protein, and the total condensed phase area all decreased, with no condensate formation observed above 300 mM KCl (Figure 2D, left).
evidence: This is shown in the salt titration experiments in Figure 2A and 2D.

claim: Electrostatic interactions play an important role in ORF1p assembly.
source: Taken together, these experiments demonstrated that purified ORF1p robustly condenses at physiological salt concentrations. Inhibition of condensation at higher salt concentrations suggests that electrostatic interactions play an important role in ORF1p assembly.
evidence: This is inferred from the salt-dependent condensation behavior shown in Figure 2A and 2D.

claim: At 300:1 protein:RNA, the ORF1p condensed phase is primarily composed of a large network of branched fibrillar structures.
source: At 300:1 protein:RNA, the ORF1p condensed phase was primarily composed of a large network of branched fibrillar structures.
evidence: This is shown in the RNA titration experiments in Figure 2B.

claim: RNA is robustly recruited to the ORF1p condensed phase at 3,000:1 protein:RNA stoichiometry.
source: When we mixed RNA with ORF1p at this stoichiometry, the labeled RNA was robustly recruited to the ORF1p condensed phase (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in the co-condensation experiments in Figure 2C.

claim: Introduction of RNA into condensates at 3,000:1 protein:RNA stoichiometry did not strongly affect the total condensate area but did significantly decrease the protein partition coefficient.
source: Introduction of RNA into condensates at this stoichiometry did not strongly affect the total condensate area but did significantly decrease the protein partition coefficient compared to the corresponding condition without RNA, suggesting that RNA may compete with ORF1p protein-protein interactions for incorporation into condensates (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: Droplets containing ORF1 protein alone exhibit slow fusion kinetics, requiring 3 min to reach a plateau of the aspect ratio.
source: Droplets containing ORF1 protein alone exhibited slow fusion kinetics, requiring 3 min to reach a plateau of the aspect ratio (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is measured from droplet fusion analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: All RNA-containing ORF1p condensates fuse more slowly than protein-only condensates.
source: All RNA-containing ORF1p condensates fused more slowly than protein-only condensates, but surprisingly this decrease was non-monotonic with increasing RNA concentration: the addition of 10,000:1 and 1,000:1 protein:RNA resulted in fusions that plateaued at high aspect ratios, while 3,000:1 RNA condensates were able to fuse to similar final aspect ratios as the ORF1p protein alone but took more time to reach the plateau (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is measured from droplet fusion analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: K3A/K4A and R261A mutant ORF1p proteins form condensed phases in buffer with physiological pH and salt concentration.
source: When reconstituted in buffer with physiological pH and salt concentration, both K3A/K4A and R261A ORF1p proteins formed condensed phases (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in the in vitro condensation assays in Figure 3A.

claim: Condensation of R261A is limited to only the conditions with higher protein concentrations and lower salt concentrations.
source: When assayed across a range of protein and salt concentrations, ORF1p K3A/K4A formed condensates in almost all of the same conditions as WT, while condensation of R261A was limited to only the conditions with higher protein concentrations and lower salt concentrations (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in the phase diagrams in Figure 3B.

claim: The protein partition coefficients of the R261A condensed phases are higher than their counterparts for WT and K3A/K4A.
source: We also noted that the protein partition coefficients of the R261A condensed phases were higher than their counterparts for WT and K3A/K4A, which further supported the hypothesis that R261 plays a role in driving ORF1p condensate assembly in the absence of RNA (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: WT ORF1p forms cellular puncta much more robustly than K3A/K4A or R261A.
source: After expressing WT, K3A/K4A, and R261A ORF1p in the context of a full-length L1 element for 6 hours in HeLa cells, we observed a stark reduction in puncta formation of the ORF1p mutants compared to WT. ORF1p K3A/K4A formed infrequent assemblies that appeared much smaller and dimmer than WT foci, while R261A staining was diffuse without any indication of condensate formation (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown in the cellular imaging experiments in Figure 3E-F.

claim: K3A/K4A and R261A mutants have undetectable retrotransposition activity.
source: The K3A/K4A and R261A mutants, however, had undetectable retrotransposition activity (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is measured by the GFP-AI retrotransposition assay shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Both K3/K4 and R261 are necessary for ORF1p condensate formation in cells and retrotransposition.
source: These findings demonstrated that both K3/K4 and R261 are necessary for ORF1p condensate formation in cells and retrotransposition, uncovering a possible connection between efficient ORF1p condensation and L1 retrotransposition activity.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined cellular and functional data for K3A/K4A and R261A mutants.

claim: The ORF1p coiled coil contains a three-residue stammer insertion (M91, E92, and L93).
source: That work also characterized a three-residue stammer insertion (M91, E92, and L93) in the ORF1p coiled coil that, when deleted, increases the stability of the coiled-coil trimer and abrogates L1 retrotransposition (Khazina and Weichenrieder, 2018).
evidence: This is cited from previous work (Khazina and Weichenrieder, 2018).

claim: Deletion of the stammer increases the stability of the coiled-coil trimer and abrogates L1 retrotransposition.
source: That work also characterized a three-residue stammer insertion (M91, E92, and L93) in the ORF1p coiled coil that, when deleted, increases the stability of the coiled-coil trimer and abrogates L1 retrotransposition (Khazina and Weichenrieder, 2018).
evidence: This is cited from previous work (Khazina and Weichenrieder, 2018).

claim: Stammer-deleted (StammerDel) ORF1p is unable to form punctate condensates in cells.
source: Indeed, when we expressed L1 with a stammer-deleted (StammerDel) ORF1p in HeLa cells, we found that the StammerDel protein was unable to form punctate condensates (Figure 4A, left two panels).
evidence: This is shown in the cellular imaging experiments in Figure 4A.

claim: Both StammerAAA and StammerAEA reconstituted stammer mutants form puncta in cells.
source: Remarkably, both reconstituted stammer mutants formed puncta in cells (Figure 4A, right two panels).
evidence: This is shown in the cellular imaging experiments in Figure 4A.

claim: Destabilizing the coiled coil of ORF1p with a three-residue stammer insertion is necessary for condensate formation in cells.
source: These experiments showed that destabilizing the coiled coil of ORF1p with a three-residue stammer insertion is necessary for condensate formation in cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the stammer deletion and reconstitution experiments shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: StammerAAA forms a similar number of puncta per cell as WT, while StammerAEA forms about half as many puncta as WT.
source: Quantifying the average number of puncta per cell confirmed the StammerDel variant's inability to form condensates and revealed that StammerAAA formed a similar number of puncta per cell as WT, while StammerAEA formed about half as many puncta as WT (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 4B.

claim: StammerDel is inactive in retrotransposition.
source: We then assayed the retrotransposition of these constructs and found that, while StammerDel was inactive, StammerAAA and StammerAEA both had readily detectable retrotransposition activity (50% of WT activity for AAA and 20% for AEA) (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is measured by the GFP-AI retrotransposition assay shown in Figure 4C.

claim: StammerAAA has 50% of WT retrotransposition activity and StammerAEA has 20% of WT retrotransposition activity.
source: We then assayed the retrotransposition of these constructs and found that, while StammerDel was inactive, StammerAAA and StammerAEA both had readily detectable retrotransposition activity (50% of WT activity for AAA and 20% for AEA) (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is measured by the GFP-AI retrotransposition assay shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Synthetic stammer insertions are capable of restoring ORF1p condensation and enable retrotransposition activity to an extent that corresponds to their relative ability to form cellular puncta.
source: These findings demonstrated that synthetic stammer insertions are capable of restoring ORF1p condensation and enable retrotransposition activity to an extent that corresponds to their relative ability to form cellular puncta.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined cellular and functional data for stammer mutants shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Efficient ORF1p condensate formation is crucial for L1 retrotransposition.
source: Together, these experiments suggest that efficient ORF1p condensate formation is crucial for L1 retrotransposition.
evidence: This is concluded from the correlation between condensation and retrotransposition activity across all mutants tested.

claim: WT and StammerAEA exhibit similar non-monotonic changes in the inverse capillary velocity of their condensed phases in response to increasing RNA concentrations.
source: Significantly, StammerAEA showed a similar non-monotonic relationship between inverse capillary velocity and RNA stoichiometry as WT, exhibiting a steep increase at the lower RNA concentration and remaining stable at the higher RNA concentration (Figure 4D, right).
evidence: This is measured from droplet fusion analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: WT and StammerAEA ORF1p exhibit distinct non-monotonic changes in the inverse capillary velocity of their in vitro condensed phases in response to increasing RNA concentration.
source: Taken together, these experiments demonstrated that WT and StammerAEA ORF1p exhibit distinct non-monotonic changes in the inverse capillary velocity of their in vitro condensed phases in response to increasing RNA concentration, suggesting that differential condensed phase material properties in the presence of varied protein-RNA stoichiometries might be important for condensate formation in cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the droplet fusion analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: WT, StammerAAA, and StammerAEA have an attenuated partitioning of RNA into ORF1p condensates with increasing protein and RNA concentrations, while R261A more strongly partitions RNA into condensates.
source: We noted that WT, StammerAAA, and, to a lesser extent, StammerAEA have an attenuated partitioning of RNA into ORF1p condensates with increasing protein and RNA concentrations, while R261A more strongly partitions RNA into condensates with increases in both protein and RNA.
evidence: This is measured from the nanomolar protein concentration experiments shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The biochemical properties of ORF1p are finely-tuned to balance protein-protein and protein-RNA interactions in a way that is critical for condensation of ORF1p in cells and downstream L1 retrotransposition.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that the biochemical properties of ORF1p are finely-tuned to balance protein-protein and protein-RNA interactions in a way that is critical for condensation of ORF1p in cells and downstream L1 retrotransposition.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined in vitro and cellular data across all mutants.

claim: ORF1p condensation in cells occurs cotranslationally, creating a viscous condensate with the L1 mRNA.
source: We propose that ORF1p condensation in cells occurs cotranslationally, creating a viscous condensate with the L1 mRNA.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the cis preference data and the minimal mixing of co-expressed ORF1p puncta.

claim: Cis-preferential L1 RNP assembly is driven by dynamical control of ORF1p co-condensation with its source RNA.
source: Cis-preferential L1 RNP assembly driven by dynamical control of ORF1p co-condensation with its source RNA is an attractive model due to the necessary spatiotemporal association between the L1 RNA and ORF1p during translation, but further work is required to understand how this type of cotranslational assembly would function on a mechanistic level.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental observations, but is acknowledged to require further investigation.

claim: L1s expressing ORF1p defective in condensation may exhibit increased trans mobilization of off-target RNAs.
source: This proposed role of ORF1p condensation in L1 RNP assembly would further imply that L1s expressing ORF1p defective in condensation may exhibit increased trans mobilization of off-target RNAs. Data supporting this hypothesis has been reported for retrotransposition of the mammalian SINE Alu, which was observed to transpose twice as efficiently when driven by an L1 with ORF1p deleted rather than an intact L1 (Dewannieux et al., 2003).
evidence: This is inferred from the cis preference model and supported by cited data on Alu mobilization.

claim: ORF1p and ORF2p are translated non-stoichiometrically, with a large excess of ORF1p.
source: The two proteins are translated non-stoichiometrically, with a large excess of ORF1p, and co-assemble with L1 mRNA to form the L1 ribonucleoprotein (RNP), which is the functional unit of L1 (Hohjoh and Singer, 1996; Taylor et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: ORF1p and ORF2p co-assemble with L1 mRNA to form the L1 ribonucleoprotein (RNP), which is the functional unit of L1.
source: The two proteins are translated non-stoichiometrically, with a large excess of ORF1p, and co-assemble with L1 mRNA to form the L1 ribonucleoprotein (RNP), which is the functional unit of L1 (Hohjoh and Singer, 1996; Taylor et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: ORF2p uses its endonuclease activity to create a single-stranded nick in the DNA and reverse transcribes the L1 mRNA into DNA using target-primed reverse transcription (TPRT).
source: Once assembled, the L1 RNP must translocate to the nucleus where ORF2p uses its endonuclease activity to create a single-stranded nick in the DNA, and reverse transcribes the L1 mRNA into DNA. The ORF2p-encoded reverse transcriptase uses the free 3'-hydroxyl of the nicked DNA as a primer, directly synthesizing the L1 complementary DNA (cDNA) into the host genome in a mechanism called target-primed reverse transcription (TPRT) (Feng et al., 1996; Cost et al., 2002; Mathias et al., 1991; Luan et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: ORF1p has nucleic acid binding activity that is necessary for L1 retrotransposition.
source: ORF1p is a 40 kDa nucleic acid binding protein that assembles into a homotrimer, and has nucleic acid binding activity that is necessary for L1 retrotransposition (Martin and Bushman, 2001; Martin et al., 2005; Kulpa and Moran, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Purified ORF1p is able to form a liquid-like condensed phase in vitro.
source: Recent work has confirmed that purified ORF1p is able to form a liquid-like condensed phase in vitro and that a truncated protein containing only the NTR and CC is sufficient for condensation (Newton et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from recent work (Newton et al., 2021).

claim: A truncated ORF1p protein containing only the NTR and CC is sufficient for condensation in vitro.
source: Recent work has confirmed that purified ORF1p is able to form a liquid-like condensed phase in vitro and that a truncated protein containing only the NTR and CC is sufficient for condensation (Newton et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from recent work (Newton et al., 2021).

claim: The tagged WT L1 element undergoes retrotransposition in approximately 1% of cells after 72 hr of expression.
source: Using a well-characterized retrotransposition paradigm that involves 72 hr of L1 expression, we found that our tagged WT element had readily detectable activity, undergoing retrotransposition in approximately 1% of cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B); this retrotransposition rate is consistent with previously reported rates for L1RP in similar constructs expressed in HeLa and HEK-293T cells (Ostertag et al., 2000; An et al., 2011).
evidence: This is measured by the GFP-AI retrotransposition assay and is consistent with published rates.

claim: L1 with ORF1-Halo has 50% of the retrotransposition activity of the untagged element.
source: L1 with ORF1-Halo has readily detectable retrotransposition activity, with 50% of the activity of the untagged element.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4B.

claim: The purified ORF1p protein is a homotrimer.
source: We modified existing protocols (Carter et al., 2020) to maximize removal of protein-bound RNA and found that the protein purified as a homotrimer as previously described (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Materials and methods).
evidence: This is shown by size exclusion chromatography in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: K3A/K4A and R261A mutant proteins are trimeric during size-exclusion chromatography.
source: Both mutants were purified using the same protocol as wild-type (WT) ORF1p and were confirmed to be trimeric during size-exclusion chromatography (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), consistent with correct overall folding and assembly of the mutant proteins.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and D.

claim: StammerAAA and StammerAEA mutant proteins are trimeric during size-exclusion chromatography.
source: Both mutants eluted from size exclusion chromatography as trimers, indicating correct folding and assembly (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and D.

claim: The monodisperse puncta seen after 6 hr of L1 induction may be more representative of ORF1p behavior at physiological expression levels than the larger stress-granule-like assemblies seen after 72 hr.
source: We observed similar stress-granule-like ORF1 condensates after inducing expression of our L1 construct for 72 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that these larger assemblies are a result of very high ORF1p expression levels, while the monodisperse puncta seen after 6 hr may be more representative of ORF1p behavior at physiological expression levels.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the morphology at different expression times shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ORF1p assemblies increase slightly in fluorescence intensity with increasing induction times, indicating that this process is not pure phase separation with a fixed saturation concentration.
source: The ORF1p assemblies also increased slightly in fluorescence intensity with increasing induction times, indicating that this process is not pure phase separation with a fixed saturation concentration (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; Flory, 1942; Huggins, 1942; Alberti et al., 2019).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and is interpreted in the context of phase separation theory.

claim: The RNA partition coefficient increases with decreasing protein concentration and increasing salt concentration.
source: Notably, we observed that the RNA partition coefficient increased with decreasing protein concentration and increasing salt concentration, indicating that more extensive protein condensation may limit RNA incorporation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: More extensive protein condensation may limit RNA incorporation into ORF1p condensates.
source: Notably, we observed that the RNA partition coefficient increased with decreasing protein concentration and increasing salt concentration, indicating that more extensive protein condensation may limit RNA incorporation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA partition coefficient data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The protein-RNA interactions that promote RNA incorporation into ORF1p condensates are in competition with protein-protein interactions that drive ORF1p partitioning.
source: These findings suggest that the protein-RNA interactions that promote RNA incorporation into ORF1p condensates are in competition with protein-protein interactions that drive ORF1p partitioning.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that RNA addition decreases protein partitioning and that increased protein concentration decreases RNA partitioning.

claim: R261A has decreased structured RNA-binding activity.
source: Mutation of a central RNA-contacting arginine, R261, was previously shown to strongly decrease ORF1p RRM-mediated RNA binding in vitro and abrogated retrotransposition activity in cells (Khazina et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from previous work (Khazina et al., 2011).

claim: K3 and K4 mutations decrease L1 retrotransposition in cells.
source: Furthermore, two lysines within this charge patch, K3 and K4, have been previously reported to decrease L1 retrotransposition in cells when mutated (Adney et al., 2019; Khazina et al., 2011; Khazina and Weichenrieder, 2018).
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: The total condensed-phase area of both K3A/K4A and R261A mutants tends to be decreased compared to WT.
source: Notably, the total condensed-phase area of both mutants tended to be decreased compared to WT, as they formed smaller and more spherical droplets, with R261A having a decreased condensate area across all conditions in which it formed droplets (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: K3A/K4A and R261A mutants robustly recruit fluorescently labeled 2-kb L1 RNA into their condensates.
source: Both mutants robustly recruited the fluorescently labeled 2-kb L1 RNA into their condensates (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The total area of R261A condensed phases increases with the addition of RNA.
source: While the addition of RNA did not appreciably change the phase diagram of WT or K3A/K4A, the total area of R261A condensed phases increased with the addition of RNA, and co-condensation with RNA allowed R261A condensates to stably form at higher salt concentrations than protein alone (Figure 3B–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B-C and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: R261A condensed phases generally have higher RNA partition coefficients than WT or K3A/K4A.
source: Additionally, the R261A condensed phases generally had higher RNA partition coefficients than WT or K3A/K4A (Figure 3D), despite the protein's reported deficiency in binding to structured RNA (Khazina et al., 2011).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Other parts of ORF1p besides R261 are able to bind RNA with a moderate affinity.
source: The recruitment of RNA to R261A condensates indicates that other parts of ORF1p are able to bind RNA with a moderate affinity, with likely areas including the disordered NTR and the N-terminal half of the coiled coil that were not included in the ORF1p constructs that initially identified R261A as a mutant with loss of RNA binding (Khazina et al., 2011).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that R261A still recruits RNA despite its known RNA-binding deficiency.

claim: The contributions of K3/K4 and R261 to ORF1 protein condensation are mechanistically distinct.
source: Enhanced condensation of R261A but not K3A/K4A with RNA addition suggests that the contributions of K3/K4 and R261 to ORF1 protein condensation are mechanistically distinct and that the partial rescue of R261A condensation with RNA is dependent on K3 and K4.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential responses of K3A/K4A and R261A to RNA addition shown in Figure 3B-D.

claim: The protein partition coefficients in matched conditions decrease with the addition of RNA for WT and R261A but not K3A/K4A.
source: Indeed, the protein partition coefficients in matched conditions decreased with the addition of RNA for WT and R261A but not K3A/K4A (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B), providing evidence for N-terminal charge patch contributions to competing protein-protein and protein-RNA interactions.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The N-terminal charge patch contributes to competing protein-protein and protein-RNA interactions.
source: Indeed, the protein partition coefficients in matched conditions decreased with the addition of RNA for WT and R261A but not K3A/K4A (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B), providing evidence for N-terminal charge patch contributions to competing protein-protein and protein-RNA interactions.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of RNA on protein partitioning across mutants shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The C-terminal half of the ORF1p coiled coil is sufficient for trimerization in vitro.
source: Previous studies characterizing the ORF1p coiled coil showed that the C-terminal half of the coiled coil is sufficient for trimerization in vitro and has a higher evolutionary conservation than the N-terminal half of the coiled coil, which was found to undergo transitions between alpha-helical and unwound states rather than maintaining the tight three-fold symmetry of the C-terminal coiled coil (Khazina et al., 2011; Khazina and Weichenrieder, 2018).
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: The N-terminal half of the ORF1p coiled coil undergoes transitions between alpha-helical and unwound states.
source: Previous studies characterizing the ORF1p coiled coil showed that the C-terminal half of the coiled coil is sufficient for trimerization in vitro and has a higher evolutionary conservation than the N-terminal half of the coiled coil, which was found to undergo transitions between alpha-helical and unwound states rather than maintaining the tight three-fold symmetry of the C-terminal coiled coil (Khazina et al., 2011; Khazina and Weichenrieder, 2018).
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: The flexibility in the coiled coil was proposed to allow ORF1p trimers to interconvert between a closed state and an open state.
source: The flexibility in the coiled coil was proposed to allow ORF1p trimers to interconvert between a closed state and an open state in which the N-terminus is capable of undergoing longer-range interactions that could facilitate inter-trimer interactions and network formation (Khazina and Weichenrieder, 2018).
evidence: This is cited from previous work (Khazina and Weichenrieder, 2018).

claim: E92 is the only stammer residue that is conserved across primate L1s.
source: We chose to specifically investigate the role of E92 because it was shown to be the only stammer residue that is conserved across primate L1s (Khazina and Weichenrieder, 2018).
evidence: This is cited from previous work (Khazina and Weichenrieder, 2018).

claim: The pattern of retrotransposition activity for stammer mutants strikingly mirrors the relative levels of puncta formation.
source: The pattern of retrotransposition activity strikingly mirrored the relative levels of puncta formation, with StammerAAA exhibiting a greater rescue of retrotransposition activity than StammerAEA, although both had less activity than WT.
evidence: This is observed by comparing Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: StammerAAA and StammerAEA form smaller, punctate condensates in response to low RNA stoichiometries.
source: Both stammer mutants exhibited decreases in their limited condensed phase areas with the addition of very low concentrations of RNA (100,000:1–3,000:1 RNA), forming punctate condensates and irregular droplet fusion intermediates that contrasted with the spherical droplets that WT formed under these conditions.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4A.

claim: The stammer mutants both form branched fibrillar condensates at 1,000:1 protein:RNA.
source: Additionally, the stammer mutants both formed branched fibrillar condensates at 1,000:1 RNA, while WT and R261A retained a morphology similar to chains of slowly fusing droplets at the same RNA concentration.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4A.

claim: K3A/K4A condensed phase transitions to a fibrillar morphology at 1,000:1 protein:RNA.
source: Similar to the stammer mutants, the ORF1p K3A/K4A condensed phase also transitioned to a fibrillar morphology at 1,000:1 RNA, despite being unaffected by lower RNA concentrations, suggesting that the N-terminal lysine residues and the stammer properties both play a role in maintaining the dynamic polymer network interactions that are necessary for spherical ORF1p-RNA co-condensates.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4A and is interpreted in the context of polymer network interactions.

claim: The N-terminal lysine residues and the stammer properties both play a role in maintaining the dynamic polymer network interactions that are necessary for spherical ORF1p-RNA co-condensates.
source: Similar to the stammer mutants, the ORF1p K3A/K4A condensed phase also transitioned to a fibrillar morphology at 1,000:1 RNA, despite being unaffected by lower RNA concentrations, suggesting that the N-terminal lysine residues and the stammer properties both play a role in maintaining the dynamic polymer network interactions that are necessary for spherical ORF1p-RNA co-condensates.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar morphological transitions of K3A/K4A and stammer mutants at high RNA concentrations.

claim: WT and StammerAEA exhibit faster fusion kinetics than the other mutants in the absence of RNA.
source: Measuring the aspect ratio of droplet fusion events over time showed that WT and StammerAEA exhibited faster fusion kinetics than the other mutants in the absence of RNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B, left).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4B.

claim: With the addition of 10,000:1 RNA, both WT and StammerAEA exhibit much slower fusion kinetics than they did in the absence of RNA.
source: However, with the addition of a very low concentration of RNA (10,000:1 RNA), both WT and StammerAEA exhibited much slower fusion kinetics than they did in the absence of RNA, while the behavior of other mutants was largely unchanged (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B, middle).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4B.

claim: K3A/K4A shows no appreciable changes in inverse capillary velocity in response to RNA.
source: K3A/K4A showed no appreciable changes in inverse capillary velocity in response to RNA (Figure 4D, middle left).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D.

claim: R261A does not exhibit a change in inverse capillary velocity at 10,000:1 RNA but has a substantial increase at 3,000:1 RNA.
source: R261A, in contrast to both, did not exhibit a change in inverse capillary velocity at the lower RNA concentration but had a substantial increase at the higher RNA concentration (Figure 4D, middle right).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D.

claim: All ORF1p variants form punctate, sub-micron assemblies at high nanomolar concentrations both in absence and presence of RNA.
source: Notably, all variants assayed formed punctate, sub-micron assemblies both in absence and presence of RNA, which appeared to be more consistent with the cellular ORF1 puncta than the previously observed droplets (Figure 4—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5A.

claim: All ORF1p variants form protein condensates that strongly colocalize with RNA at nanomolar protein concentrations.
source: While all variants formed protein condensates that strongly colocalized with RNA, R261A was the only variant that had lower colocalization at the higher RNA stoichiometry, which was likely due to the formation of RNA foci with protein content that was below our limit of detection (Figure 4—figure supplement 5A–B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5B.

claim: R261A is the only variant that has lower colocalization at the higher RNA stoichiometry.
source: While all variants formed protein condensates that strongly colocalized with RNA, R261A was the only variant that had lower colocalization at the higher RNA stoichiometry, which was likely due to the formation of RNA foci with protein content that was below our limit of detection (Figure 4—figure supplement 5A–B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5B.

claim: The RNA partitioning behaviors across ORF1p variants parallel the trends observed for the material properties of ORF1p-RNA condensates across protein-RNA stoichiometries.
source: Notably, the RNA partitioning behaviors across ORF1p variants paralleled the trends observed for the material properties of ORF1p-RNA condensates across protein-RNA stoichiometries, suggesting that the differential fusion properties across variants are due to differences in protein and RNA partitioning at the tested stoichiometries.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the RNA partitioning data in Figure 4E with the fusion kinetics data in Figure 4D.

claim: The differential fusion properties across ORF1p variants are due to differences in protein and RNA partitioning at the tested stoichiometries.
source: Notably, the RNA partitioning behaviors across ORF1p variants paralleled the trends observed for the material properties of ORF1p-RNA condensates across protein-RNA stoichiometries, suggesting that the differential fusion properties across variants are due to differences in protein and RNA partitioning at the tested stoichiometries.
evidence: This is inferred from the parallel trends in RNA partitioning and fusion kinetics.

claim: ORF1p's major role in retrotransposition is thought to involve the formation of an RNP with the L1 mRNA and ORF2p in the cytoplasm.
source: Although ORF1p's major role in retrotransposition is thought to involve the formation of an RNP with the L1 mRNA and ORF2p in the cytoplasm, the diversity of ORF1p mutations that abrogate retrotransposition suggests the possibility of additional roles, including mediating RNP interactions with host proteins and participation in the downstream steps of nuclear translocation, DNA search for integration sites, or reverse transcription and integration (Martin et al., 2005; Kulpa and Moran, 2005; Khazina et al., 2011; Taylor et al., 2013; Khazina and Weichenrieder, 2018; Taylor et al., 2018; Adney et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is based on established knowledge and citations.

claim: The diversity of ORF1p mutations that abrogate retrotransposition suggests the possibility of additional roles for ORF1p beyond RNP formation.
source: Although ORF1p's major role in retrotransposition is thought to involve the formation of an RNP with the L1 mRNA and ORF2p in the cytoplasm, the diversity of ORF1p mutations that abrogate retrotransposition suggests the possibility of additional roles, including mediating RNP interactions with host proteins and participation in the downstream steps of nuclear translocation, DNA search for integration sites, or reverse transcription and integration (Martin et al., 2005; Kulpa and Moran, 2005; Khazina et al., 2011; Taylor et al., 2013; Khazina and Weichenrieder, 2018; Taylor et al., 2018; Adney et al., 2019).
evidence: This is inferred from the diversity of mutations affecting retrotransposition and is supported by citations.

claim: The minimal mixing observed for co-expressed fluorescent ORF1p puncta provides a biophysical mechanism for L1 cis preference.
source: The minimal mixing observed for co-expressed fluorescent ORF1p puncta suggests that the physical properties of these assemblies minimize fusion events and protein exchange with the surrounding cytoplasm, providing a biophysical mechanism for L1 cis preference (Figure 1E–G, Figure 4D–E).
evidence: This is inferred from the colocalization data in Figure 1E-G and the material properties data in Figure 4D-E.

claim: Kinetically arrested condensates can allow for the coexistence of many small condensates at low, endogenous concentrations.
source: This type of kinetically arrested condensate has been described in simulations and has been proposed as a mechanism for the coexistence of many small condensates at low, endogenous concentrations, rather than the thermodynamic expectation that the condensates would coalesce into a single, large equilibrium-like assembly (Ranganathan and Shakhnovich, 2020; Mittag and Pappu, 2022).
evidence: This is cited from theoretical work on condensate behavior.

claim: A mechanism involving reversible co-condensation of ORF1p together with the L1 RNA from which it was translated would allow for cis substrate preference without sequence-specific RNA binding.
source: A mechanism involving reversible co-condensation of ORF1p together with the L1 RNA from which it was translated would allow for cis substrate preference without sequence-specific RNA binding (Kolosha and Martin, 2003).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental observations and is supported by a citation.

claim: Disrupting the spatiotemporal regulation of expression of an RNA-binding protein and the RNAs it condenses with can abrogate the formation of compositionally distinct condensates.
source: Recent work has provided cellular evidence that disrupting the spatiotemporal regulation of expression of an RNA-binding protein and the RNAs it condenses with can abrogate the formation of compositionally distinct condensates, emphasizing the importance of dynamical control of protein-RNA co-condensation in cells (Lin et al., 2023).
evidence: This is cited from recent work (Lin et al., 2023).

claim: Cotranslational condensation of ORF1p with its cis RNA would require initial low concentrations of protein to favor protein-protein assembly while limiting protein-RNA condensation.
source: Cotranslational condensation of ORF1p with its cis RNA would also require initial low concentrations of protein to favor protein-protein assembly while limiting protein-RNA condensation to avoid incorporating non-template RNA molecules in the L1 RNP, which we found to be another shared feature of the ORF1p variants that underwent condensation in cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA partitioning data in Figure 4E and the proposed cotranslational assembly model.

claim: The behavior of ORF1p condensates in biochemical reconstitution experiments is distinct from the puncta properties observed in cells.
source: The behavior of ORF1p condensates in biochemical reconstitution experiments was distinct from the puncta properties observed in cells. In particular, the extensive droplet-like phase and the droplet fusion events seen in reconstituted ORF1p contrasted with the uniform punctate morphology and lack of mixing seen in cells.
evidence: This is observed by comparing the in vitro data (Figure 2) with the cellular data (Figure 1).

claim: Reducing protein concentrations and titrating RNA concentrations allows for better approximation of the punctate condensates seen in cells.
source: We found that reducing protein concentrations and titrating RNA concentrations allowed us to better approximate the punctate condensates seen in cells (Figure 2B, Figure 4—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is shown by comparing the in vitro data at different protein and RNA concentrations with cellular observations.

claim: The discrepancies between in vitro and cellular ORF1p behavior are likely due to a dynamical control mechanism in cells that is not reflected in the reconstituted system.
source: While we posit that the discrepancies we observe are due to a dynamical control mechanism in cells that is not reflected in our reconstituted system (Lin et al., 2023), there are many other buffer parameters and non-equilibrium processes in cells that could play a role in modifying ORF1p assembly kinetics, including macromolecular crowding, ATP hydrolysis, and post-translational modifications (Khan et al., 2018; Delarue et al., 2018; Brangwynne et al., 2011; Brangwynne, 2011; Nott et al., 2015; Aumiller and Keating, 2016; Carlson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for the differences between in vitro and cellular observations, supported by citations.

claim: The ORF1 mutants in this study indicate that ORF1p condensation is critical for L1 retrotransposition.
source: The ORF1 mutants in this study indicate that ORF1p condensation is critical for L1 retrotransposition.
evidence: This is concluded from the correlation between condensation defects and loss of retrotransposition across all mutants tested.

claim: A truncated ORF1p containing just the NTR and coiled coil (residues 1–152; NTR-CC) is sufficient for condensation in vitro.
source: The authors additionally demonstrated that a truncated ORF1p containing just the disordered NTR and coiled coil (residues 1–152; NTR-CC) is sufficient for condensation.
evidence: This is cited from Newton et al., 2021.

claim: Both ORF1p R261A and the truncated NTR-CC protein likely undergo condensation in vitro through a mechanism similar to complex coacervation.
source: We predict that both ORF1p R261A and the truncated NTR-CC protein undergo condensation in vitro through a mechanism similar to complex coacervation, which requires only unstructured charge-charge interactions (Aumiller and Keating, 2016; Boeynaems et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the properties of R261A and NTR-CC and the known mechanisms of complex coacervation.

claim: The ORF1p RRM participates in protein-protein interactions that drive condensation in the absence of RNA.
source: Our data suggest that the ORF1p RRM participates in protein-protein interactions that drive condensation in the absence of RNA, while the unstructured NTR plays a smaller role in protein-only condensation (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the behavior of R261A which has a defective RRM but can still condense, though less efficiently than WT.

claim: The unstructured NTR plays a smaller role in protein-only condensation than the RRM.
source: Our data suggest that the ORF1p RRM participates in protein-protein interactions that drive condensation in the absence of RNA, while the unstructured NTR plays a smaller role in protein-only condensation (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the behavior of K3A/K4A which has defects in the NTR but condenses similarly to WT in most conditions.

claim: The NTR basic patch allows for stark modulation of the physical properties of the condensate in response to low stoichiometries of RNA.
source: However, the NTR charge patch allows for stark modulation of the physical properties of the condensate in response to low stoichiometries of RNA (Figure 4D), which is critical for condensation in cells (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: This is shown by the differential response of WT and K3A/K4A to RNA in fusion kinetics experiments (Figure 4D) and cellular condensation (Figure 3E-F).

claim: The RRM downregulates the incorporation of RNA into the co-condensates.
source: The RRM has lesser contributions to the physical properties of ORF1p-RNA condensates but appears to downregulate the incorporation of RNA into the co-condensates (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), and we find that the combination of protein-protein and protein-RNA interactions of both the NTR basic patch and the RRM drives the formation of a condensate that is highly sensitive to very low RNA concentrations (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: This is inferred from the higher RNA partition coefficients of R261A compared to WT shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The combination of protein-protein and protein-RNA interactions of both the NTR basic patch and the RRM drives the formation of a condensate that is highly sensitive to very low RNA concentrations.
source: The RRM has lesser contributions to the physical properties of ORF1p-RNA condensates but appears to downregulate the incorporation of RNA into the co-condensates (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), and we find that the combination of protein-protein and protein-RNA interactions of both the NTR basic patch and the RRM drives the formation of a condensate that is highly sensitive to very low RNA concentrations (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: This is concluded from the combined data on WT, K3A/K4A, and R261A behavior across different RNA concentrations.

claim: The flexibility of the coiled coil that separates the NTR and RRM is critical to the roles of the NTR and RRM in condensation.
source: Furthermore, the flexibility of the coiled coil that separates these two motifs appears to be critical to the roles of the NTR and RRM in condensation, since the StammerDel mutant that has a more rigid coiled coil (Khazina and Weichenrieder, 2018) exhibits starkly reduced assembly in cells (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of condensation in StammerDel and its rescue by stammer reconstitution.

claim: Two distinctive basic motifs and a flexible coiled-coil scaffold allow ORF1p to undergo rapid, dynamically controlled condensation with cis RNA within the complex environment of the cell.
source: In this way, we propose that two distinctive basic motifs and a flexible coiled-coil scaffold allow ORF1p to undergo rapid, dynamically controlled condensation with cis RNA within the complex environment of the cell.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the combined data from all mutants and experimental conditions.
